title: Non-Freaked Out Common Core — Part 4 — Argument and Debate
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: The fourth installment of Stuart's non-freaked out Common Core series makes a single high-leverage recommendation: have students argue, frequently, in every subject. He grounds it in Graff and Schmoker's 2011 warning that argument's 'special place' in the CCSS is buried in an appendix and will be diluted if teachers try to teach all ten writing anchor standards equally. His four-part approach is to go big on written and spoken argument, exploit the link between the two, and have students speak and write frequently. He then gets specific about what students must internalize — a claim is a debatable point, arguers back claims with evidence and logic and explain the connection, and the best arguers can argue both sides and anticipate counterclaims. The centerpiece is a minute-by-minute walkthrough of a full class debate on 'Does power always corrupt?' built around Animal Farm and world history, from a five-minute topicality framing through brainstorming, research, random team assignment, the debate itself, student reflection and teacher feedback. He then introduces the pop-up debate — students stand at their seats when ready, graded on paraphrasing the previous speaker and supporting their own point — as the format with the best return. He ends by saying he would keep debating even if the Common Core vanished tomorrow.
points: The structural argument: because the CCSS signals argument's priority only by putting W.CCR.1 first and burying the rationale in an appendix, teachers spread themselves across ten writing standards and lose the highest-impact one.
Stuart insists the spoken-written link is the accessibility lever — students who can enjoy and win classroom debates start to see why crafted written arguments matter.

The pop-up debate is his most transferable format: no teams, no moving seats, students stand when ready, and the grading targets exactly two moves — paraphrase the previous speaker, then make your own evidence-backed point.

His debate lesson is engineered against the usual failure modes — a defined topic and defined terms up front ('topicality'), independent brainstorming before collaborative, and a rule that someone new must speak each round.

His closing case for debate is non-instrumental: it changes how students see the world, forces them to hold both sides of an issue, and transforms the task of reading and writing arguments — Common Core or no Common Core.
quotes: But don't just take my word for it. In an article back in 2011, gurus Jerry Graff and Mike Schmoker (their books Clueless in Academe, They Say / I Say, and Focus have hugely shaped me) warned that, though the CCSS held promise, especially compared to the preceding generation of state-created wish lists, there was still too much fluff. Their fear was that the high impact standard of argument might get watered down amongst the rest.

This is problematic; many will not read the appendices and, as a result, will likely spread their curriculum too thin by trying to equally teach all 10 of the basic writing anchor standards. The simple problem with trying to equally teach all 10 is that, frankly, it can't be done well, at least not by an average teacher like me.

Emphasize and exploit the strong link between spoken and written argumentation. I think this is one of the keys for making argumentative writing accessible. When students can enjoy, participate, and dominate in classroom debates, they begin to see and understand the beauty of crafting great arguments in writing.

From the first day to the last, we simply do lots of arguing. I've found no activity besides reading and writing that match it for the power to enhance my students' self-concepts, academic abilities, and character strengths. Seriously.

Below, I'll walk you through the lesson for the day of the debate; for what it's worth, this was one of the best debates I've yet seen. Remember, the reason debates work well in my class is because I invest a good amount of time into them throughout the year — it's not because I'm some magical debate coach.

Teacher feedback (5 minutes): I then give students what I noticed. I use specific examples and student names, and I both praise and critique. This is a time for us to get better, not a time to give fake praise or avoid the truth.

I've found this to be an especially effective format when I grade them on two croosch moves: 1) their ability to paraphrase the speaker they are responding to, and 2) their ability to make their own point with support from evidence and/or logic. After doing this form of debate last Friday, I caught my students paraphrasing in a much less structured classroom discussion this week.
